title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Maya Patel
summary: Canonical engineering standards for API design, code quality, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. Includes decision records (ADRs) for cross-cutting architecture choices and an appendix with example configs and rollout checklists.
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. Its goal is to provide a single, opinionated reference for engineering teams building production inference services and client-facing APIs. The guidance below is normative: new services and significant changes should reference these standards and record deviations as ADRs.

Scope

- Applies to all services owned by the inference platform, control plane, and customer-facing APIs.
- Includes hosted, dedicated, and private deployment modes.
- Covers design, implementation, operational thresholds, and rollout procedures.

Principles (high level)

1. Developer ergonomics: APIs must be simple and consistent to encourage secure, correct usage.
2. Predictable economics: designs must enable clear unit-cost accounting (tokens, GPU-hours).
3. Production-first: defaults must prioritize reliability and observability over experimentation.
4. Least surprise: consistent error semantics and retry behaviors across services.
5. Documented exceptions: any deviation requires an ADR owned by the service owner.

1) API Standards

Purpose: Ensure consistent, stable, and simple APIs for internal and external consumers.

- API surface: REST + JSON for external endpoints, gRPC for high-throughput internal RPCs.
- Versioning: Use semantic versioning for public API routes (v1, v2). Major changes require migration docs and a two-release deprecation window.
- Contracts: Request/response schemas must be defined in OpenAPI (external) or proto files (internal) and stored in the API schema registry.
- Idempotency: All mutating operations must accept an idempotency key header (Idempotency-Key).
- Error model: Standard error envelope {"code":"STRING","message":"STRING","details":[]} with stable error codes documented in the API spec. HTTP status mapping: 4xx = client error, 5xx = server error. 429 for rate limits.
- Rate limits: Default per-API plan limits applied in the gateway; services should return Retry-After.
- Authentication: OAuth2 for user-facing dashboards; mTLS or API keys for service-to-service auth. Keys rotated via KMS automated rotation.
- Telemetry: Every API handler must emit structured request logs with fields: service, route, model_id, tenant_id, request_size_tokens, response_size_tokens, latency_ms, status.

Example OpenAPI fragment (stored in registry):

    paths:
      /v1/generate:
        post:
          summary: Generate text
          requestBody:
            content:
              application/json:
                schema:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/GenerateRequest'

2) Coding Standards

- Languages: Primary backend languages are Go (core runtime, routing), Python (orchestrations, ML helpers), and TypeScript (console/frontend).
- Style: Adopt gofmt/golangci-lint, black + ruff for Python, and eslint + prettier for TypeScript.
- Testing: Unit test coverage minimum 60% for new modules; critical path components (scheduling, billing, auth) 85%+.
- Static checks: Enforce type checks (mypy/typed-ast for Python, strict typescript), security linting (Snyk or equivalent), and dependency pinning.
- Code review: Two approvers for public API changes and infra changes; one approver for minor internal fixes.
- Secrets: No secrets in code; use secret manager + environment injection. PRs that add third-party libs must include an SBOM update.

3) Infrastructure Standards

- IaC: All infra defined via Terraform modules in the org repo. Modules must be idempotent and documented with inputs/outputs.
- Environments: Staging mirrors production network and capacity shapes. Feature branches can deploy ephemeral stacks via CI.
- Networking: Service mesh (Envoy + xDS) for intra-cluster routing; mTLS enforced for all service-to-service traffic.
- Capacity: GPU fleet configured in pools: serving, warm-standby, and canary. Autoscaling rules defined per-pool with clear surge caps.
- CI/CD: Git-based trunk with main protected; release pipelines produce immutable artifacts (container images with digest).
- Backup & Recovery: Daily DB backups with 30-day retention; RTO target for control-plane metadata 6 hours.

Example Terraform policy snippet (documented in registry):

    module "gke_cluster" {
      source = "git::ssh://git@repo/infra-modules.git//gke"
      name   = "redwood-prod-1"
    }

4) Model-Serving Standards

- Model artifacts: Models tracked in the model registry with metadata: model_id, version, architecture, quantization_profile, input_schema, kv_cache_compatibility.
- Docker images: Serving runtime images must be minimal, non-root, and scanned for CVEs.
- Interfaces: Serving endpoints accept the standard inference request envelope and produce structured outputs. Binary payloads (if used) encoded as base64 and schema-documented.
- Quantized variants: All quantized model variants must document the expected quality delta vs float baseline (P0 metrics).
- Routing: Smart routing policy configuration files specify latency SLO and cost target. Fallbacks (cheaper or lower-latency variants) defined per-model.
- Canaries & rollouts: Canary traffic 1-5% for 24 hours with automatic rollback on quality or error regressions. See rollout checklist below.

Rollout checklist (model deployments):

1. Register model and upload artifacts to model registry.
2. Run QA evals using standard prompt sets (applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks).
3. Publish canary with 1% traffic; monitor SLOs and eval metrics for 24h.
4. Gradually increase to 10% over 24h.
5. Full rollout if no regressions; otherwise rollback and open regression triage.

5) Observability Standards

- Metrics: Use Prometheus for metrics ingestion. Standard metric names and labels documented in the metrics catalog. Required metrics for services: request_rate, error_rate, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, tokens_consumed.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry tracing enabled in all services with the following required spans: api.request, model.encode, model.decode, kv_cache.lookup, scheduler.queue. Capture tenant_id and request_id as trace tags.
- Logs: Structured JSON logs emitted to central logging; index fields include timestamp, level, service, route, trace_id, request_id, tenant_id.
- Dashboards: Per-service SLO dashboards: latency distribution, error budget burn, token costs by route, and model quality regressions.
- Alerts: PagerDuty alerts for SLO burn > 20% within 1 hour, error_rate > 1% sustained for 5 minutes, and p95_latency exceeding SLO by 50% for 10 minutes.

Alert example (Prometheus rule):

    - alert: HighErrorRate
      expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="service-x",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="service-x"}[5m])) > 0.01
      for: 5m
      labels:
        severity: page

6) Performance Standards

- SLOs: Default public API SLOs: 99.5% for request success within configured latency; p95 latency targets per route must be documented in the service README.
- Tail latency: p99 target must be no more than 3x p95 for interactive endpoints.
- Throughput: Batching policies must be configurable and default to dynamic batching tuned by historical request size distribution.
- Cost: Every model-route must publish an estimated token-cost-per-1000 and GPU-cost-per-hour in its service metadata.
- Benchmarks: New model variants must include benchmark results for cold start, steady-state throughput, and kv-cache hit/miss scenarios. Include representative sequence length distributions.

7) ADRs (Decision Records)

Pattern: Use lightweight Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) for any cross-cutting platform decision (choice of RPC framework, standardizing quantization formats, global routing policy). ADRs must be stored in the architecture repo and referenced from service READMEs.

Required ADR metadata: title, context, decision, consequences, owner, date, status. ADRs are short (1–2 pages).

Recent/Required ADRs (examples):

- ADR-2025-11-01: Standardize internal RPC on gRPC over TLS — decision: adopt gRPC for high-throughput internal calls; consequences: protobuf-first design, added dependency but improved performance. Owner: eng-platform.
- ADR-2026-01-18: Quantization interchange format — decision: adopt QF-1 (internal spec) as canonical quantized model metadata. Owner: applied-ml-and-evals.

ADRs Process:

1. Propose: Create ADR draft in the architecture ADRs folder.
2. Review: Solicit reviewers from eng-platform, eng-serving-runtime, and security.
3. Record: Publish ADR and update related code/docs.

Appendix: Example service-level config and rollout checklist

Service config (yaml):

    service_name: "model-serve-api"
    routes:
      - path: "/v1/generate"
        model_id: "redwood/llama-xxl:2026-02"
        batching:
          enabled: true
          max_batch_size: 64
          max_latency_ms: 50
        routing_policy:
          latency_slo_ms: 200
          cost_target_cents_per_1k_tokens: 3

Rollout checklist (minimum):

- Unit & integration tests pass in CI (green).
- Benchmarks uploaded and within accepted delta from baseline.
- Canary metrics monitored for 48 hours with no SLO or quality regressions.
- Security review completed for new dependencies.
- Documentation updated (README, OpenAPI).

Ownership and compliance

- Each service team is responsible for ensuring compliance with this doc.
- Platform Architecture (eng-platform) owns the ADRs index and the canonical metrics catalog.
- Security owns network-level policies and secret management practices.

Deviations and exceptions

- Short-lived exceptions may be documented in team RFCs, but persistent deviations require an ADR.
- Emergency deviations (e.g., to mitigate production incidents) must be retroactively recorded as an ADR within 2 weeks.

Frequently asked questions

Q: When should I choose REST vs gRPC?
A: Use REST for external customer-facing APIs and gRPC for high-throughput internal RPCs where low-latency and streaming are required.

Q: How do we measure quality regressions for model rollouts?
A: Use the standard eval harness (applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness) linked in the model registry to run prompt-set-based comparisons and monitor key metrics (accuracy, toxicity, hallucination rate) defined per model.
